plan: Complete enhanced-ACT natural-science passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000035, 'What the Stripes Are For'), about 600 words, on competing explanations for zebra stripes (2016 vision study vs camouflage; 2014 range analysis and 2019 farm experiments for the fly hypothesis). Topic checked against every ACT Reading passage's opening and all verbal bank titles (no zebra or stripe passage). 9 questions weighted toward reasoning about evidence (control group, correlation vs cause, weakening).

passages.title: What the Stripes Are For
passages.text:
Few animal patterns are as familiar as a zebra's stripes, and few have provoked as many explanations. For more than a century, biologists have proposed reasons that a horselike animal grazing on open grassland might benefit from bold black and white bands. The stripes might hide zebras from predators, confuse a lion in mid-chase, help the animals stay cool, or allow zebras to recognize one another. Each idea has had its champions. Until recently, few had been tested in ways that could tell them apart.

The camouflage idea faced an obvious objection: to a human observer, a zebra on a plain is anything but hidden. Defenders replied that lions and hyenas do not see the way people do. A study published in 2016 took that reply seriously. Its authors used what is known about the sharpness of lions', hyenas', and zebras' vision to estimate the distances at which stripes could be made out at all. In daylight, they concluded, a lion could resolve the stripes only from within about fifty meters, close enough that it would probably already have heard or smelled its prey. Farther away, the stripes would blur into a uniform gray that offered no special concealment. At dusk, when lions often hunt, the distances shrank further.

Another idea, long treated as a curiosity, concerned insects. In Africa, horseflies and other biting flies carry diseases that can be fatal to horses and their relatives, and a zebra's short coat offers little protection against them. A 2014 analysis compared the ranges of living horse species with dozens of environmental factors and found that striping was most closely associated not with predators or heat but with the regions where biting flies are most active.

Correlation, though, could not show that the stripes did anything. So in 2019 a team watched horseflies approach zebras and ordinary horses kept at the same farm in Britain. The flies circled both kinds of animals about equally often. But they landed on the zebras far less often; many seemed to fly in too fast, bump against the zebra, and bounce off, as though they had failed to slow down for a landing. The researchers then dressed horses in coats of different patterns. Flies landed much less often on horses wearing striped coats than on the same horses wearing plain black or plain white coats, yet the horses' uncovered heads were landed on about equally often whatever coat the animal wore.

None of this proves that flies are the only reason zebras are striped. A trait can serve more than one purpose, and some researchers think the stripes may also matter for heat or for social life. But the fly hypothesis has something its rivals have so far lacked: experiments in which the pattern was the only thing that changed, and the animals' experience changed with it. Exactly how stripes throw off a landing fly remains uncertain. One possibility is that bold, repeating bands disrupt the way a fly judges its speed as it closes in on a surface.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Zebra stripes evolved mainly to hide zebras from lions and hyenas on open plains.
choices.B: Scientists have now shown that zebra stripes serve only a single purpose.
choices.C: Studies of zebras show that correlations are useless as scientific evidence.
choices.D: The idea that stripes deter biting flies now has the most support.

candidates.evidence: the fly hypothesis has something its rivals have so far lacked
candidates.explanation: The passage surveys several explanations, reports evidence against camouflage, and presents correlational and experimental support for the fly hypothesis, while noting that other functions are not ruled out.

A.rationale: Paragraph 2 reports evidence against the camouflage idea.

B.rationale: Paragraph 5 says flies may not be 'the only reason.'

C.rationale: Paragraph 4 says correlation alone could not show cause, not that it is useless.

hints: Which explanation does the passage spend the most time supporting?

strategy.explanation: Summarize where the passage ends up.

candidates.remember: A main idea must fit the passage's qualifications as well as its conclusion.

candidates.stem: The last sentence of the first paragraph ("Until recently, few had been tested in ways that could tell them apart") mainly serves to:

choices.A: set up the passage's focus on evidence that can distinguish among the explanations.
choices.B: suggest that most of the explanations listed have already been disproved.
choices.C: explain why biologists lost interest in zebra stripes for many years.
choices.D: introduce a new explanation that none of the earlier biologists had considered.

candidates.evidence: Until recently, few had been tested in ways that could tell them apart.
candidates.explanation: The rest of the passage describes studies (the 2016 vision study, the 2014 analysis, the 2019 experiments) that can separate one explanation from another, which this sentence anticipates.

B.rationale: The sentence says the ideas had not been tested, not that they had been disproved.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests interest declined; the paragraph says the ideas had champions.

D.rationale: The passage tests ideas already listed, including the fly idea.

hints: What do the following paragraphs describe?

strategy.explanation: Connect the sentence to what comes next.

candidates.remember: A paragraph's last sentence often previews the rest of the passage.

candidates.stem: In the second paragraph, the statement that the 2016 study "took that reply seriously" most nearly means that the study's authors:

choices.A: agreed that zebras are well hidden from predators.
choices.B: tested the defenders' claim instead of dismissing it.
choices.C: argued that camouflage should be judged by human vision.
choices.D: measured how far away lions can hear and smell prey.

candidates.evidence: Its authors used what is known about the sharpness of lions', hyenas', and zebras' vision
candidates.explanation: The defenders' reply was that predators see differently from people; the study checked that reply by estimating what lions and hyenas could actually see.

A.rationale: The study's conclusion went against the camouflage idea.

C.rationale: The study used predators' vision, not human vision.

D.rationale: The study measured how far away stripes could be seen.

strategy.explanation: Find the reply in the sentence before.

candidates.remember: Taking a claim seriously means testing it, not necessarily agreeing with it.

candidates.subskill: Purpose of a detail in an argument
candidates.stem: The detail that a lion within about fifty meters "would probably already have heard or smelled its prey" (paragraph 2) mainly supports the idea that:

choices.A: lions depend more on smell than on sight in every hunting situation.
choices.B: lions hunt mostly at dusk because their hearing is better at night.
choices.C: stripes would add little concealment even where a lion can see them.
choices.D: zebras can usually detect a lion before the lion detects them.

candidates.evidence: close enough that it would probably already have heard or smelled its prey
candidates.explanation: Within fifty meters the lion could see stripes, but by then it would likely have found the zebra by sound or smell anyway; beyond that, the stripes blur. So stripes would hide a zebra neither near nor far.

A.rationale: The detail concerns one distance, not lions' senses in general.

B.rationale: Dusk hunting is mentioned only to note that stripe distances shrink.

D.rationale: The passage says nothing about which animal notices the other first.

hints: What would the lion already know at fifty meters?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the detail rules out.

candidates.remember: A detail can close off the last escape for a weakened claim.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must see that the detail answers the remaining case (near distances), completing the argument against camouflage.

candidates.subskill: Limits of a type of evidence
candidates.stem: Based on paragraphs 3 and 4, why did the 2014 analysis not settle whether stripes protect zebras from flies?

choices.A: It linked stripes to fly-rich regions without showing that stripes reduce bites.
choices.B: It studied horse species that do not live where biting flies are common.
choices.C: It found that predators were more closely linked to striping than flies were.
choices.D: It considered only a single environmental factor in its comparison of species.

candidates.evidence: Correlation, though, could not show that the stripes did anything.
candidates.explanation: The 2014 study found an association between striping and fly-rich regions. Paragraph 4 explains that this correlation could not show that the stripes had any effect, which is why experiments followed.

B.rationale: It compared species across many regions, including those where flies are most active.

C.rationale: It found the reverse: flies, not predators, were most closely associated with striping.

hints: What does paragraph 4 say correlation could not show?

strategy.explanation: Read the first sentence of paragraph 4.

candidates.remember: A correlation shows that two things occur together, not that one causes the other.

candidates.stem: The observation that flies circled zebras and horses "about equally often" (paragraph 4) suggests that the stripes:

choices.A: make zebras harder for flies to locate from a distance.
choices.B: attract more flies to zebras than plain coats attract to horses.
choices.C: have no effect on how flies behave around zebras.
choices.D: do not stop flies from finding zebras but disrupt their landings.

candidates.evidence: But they landed on the zebras far less often
candidates.explanation: Equal circling shows the flies found both animals; far fewer landings on zebras shows the stripes mattered only at the final approach.

A.rationale: Equal circling means the flies found zebras as readily as horses.

B.rationale: Flies circled both about equally, not more around zebras.

C.rationale: Flies landed on zebras far less often, so the stripes had an effect.

hints: What differed between zebras and horses, and what did not?
candidates.remember: Separate what stayed the same from what changed.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must combine the equal-circling and unequal-landing observations; the 'harder to locate' choice reverses the first.

candidates.subskill: Purpose of a control in an experiment
candidates.stem: The detail that the horses' uncovered heads "were landed on about equally often whatever coat the animal wore" (paragraph 4) is significant mainly because it shows that:

choices.A: the fewer landings came from the coats' pattern, not the horses.
choices.B: biting flies prefer to land on an animal's head rather than its body.
choices.C: a striped coat protects every part of a horse's body from flies.
choices.D: the horses found the patterned coats uncomfortable to wear.

candidates.evidence: yet the horses' uncovered heads were landed on about equally often whatever coat the animal wore
candidates.explanation: If flies avoided the horses for some other reason (smell or behavior), the heads would also have been landed on less. Because heads were landed on equally, the difference on the body must come from the coat's pattern.

B.rationale: The passage compares heads across coats, not heads with bodies.

C.rationale: The heads were uncovered and got no protection.

D.rationale: Nothing is said about the horses' comfort.

hints: What would the heads show if the flies were avoiding the horses for another reason?

strategy.explanation: Think of the heads as a comparison group.

candidates.remember: An unchanged part of an experiment helps rule out other explanations.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must recognize a built-in control; the 'protects every part' choice misreads the uncovered heads.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 1, the word "champions" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: Each idea has had its champions.
candidates.explanation: To champion an idea is to argue for it; each explanation has had scientists who supported it.

A.rationale: This is a familiar meaning, but the ideas have people who argue for them, not victories.

B.rationale: The ideas compete with one another, but their champions are those who favor them.

D.rationale: Critics would oppose an idea, the opposite of championing it.

hints: Who would an idea's champions be?

strategy.explanation: Predict a word for people who favor an idea.

candidates.remember: Check whether the familiar meaning fits the sentence before choosing it.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating evidence that would weaken a claim
candidates.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most directly weaken the fly hypothesis as the passage presents it?

choices.A: Lions turned out to see stripes clearly from much farther than fifty meters.
choices.B: Stripes turned out to help zebras recognize members of their own herd.
choices.C: Flies turned out to circle zebras slightly more often than they circle horses.
choices.D: The most boldly striped zebras turned out to live where biting flies are rare.

candidates.evidence: striping was most closely associated not with predators or heat but with the regions where biting flies are most active
candidates.explanation: The fly hypothesis draws support from the 2014 link between striping and fly-rich regions. Finding the boldest stripes where flies are rare would contradict that evidence.

A.rationale: This bears on the camouflage idea, not on the fly hypothesis.

B.rationale: The passage says a trait can serve more than one purpose, so this would not undercut the fly idea.

C.rationale: The fly hypothesis rests on landings, which this finding does not address.

hints: Which evidence supports the fly hypothesis?

strategy.explanation: Ask which choices even concern the fly hypothesis.

candidates.remember: To weaken a claim, contradict the evidence it rests on.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must identify which evidence supports the fly hypothesis and reject findings about other hypotheses or compatible functions.
